interviewQuestions.question: Which pattern is behind dependency injection?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd start by naming that DI itself is a technique, not one of the GoF patterns — it's Dependency Inversion applied at construction time. The pattern actually doing the work underneath a DI container is a Factory, or an Abstract Factory for a whole family of related dependencies: when the container resolves a class's constructor and sees it needs some interface, it's deciding which concrete implementation to construct and supplying it, exactly like a hand-written factory method would.

I'd make the comparison concrete: manually, you'd write a static method that constructs a PaymentGateway and passes it into PaymentService's constructor. A DI container does the same thing, just generated and run automatically for every class in your object graph instead of hand-written per class.

I'd close by naming that the container's scope handling (singleton vs per-request) isn't a new pattern either — it's a container-managed Singleton.

**Testing:** whether you understand DI isn't magic — it's familiar patterns automated at scale.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: The pattern underneath a DI container

interviewQuestions.question: Is Service Locator the same thing as Dependency Injection?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
No, and I'd explain the difference by direction of control rather than just asserting they're different. DI pushes a dependency into a class through its constructor — the class's public interface visibly declares what it needs. Service Locator has the class pull its dependency by calling out to a global registry from inside a method body, so the dependency never appears in the constructor and is only discoverable by reading the implementation.

I'd use the one-line version: DI is push, Service Locator is pull — and that difference is exactly why DI is the preferred default despite both technically solving 'how do I get an instance of X.'

**Testing:** whether you understand these as genuinely different approaches, not two names for the same idea.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Service Locator vs Dependency Injection

interviewQuestions.question: What pattern handles object lifetime — like singleton vs per-request scope — inside a DI container?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd explain that this is a container-managed Singleton, not a new pattern. Registering a bean as singleton-scoped means the container constructs it exactly once and hands out that same instance to every dependent that asks for it — the same one-instance guarantee a hand-rolled Singleton provides.

The difference that actually matters: the container's version sidesteps the usual Singleton testability problem, since the container can substitute a different instance for tests without touching any production code, unlike a hardcoded static getInstance() call.

For request- or prototype-scoped beans, I'd explain it's the same underlying Factory mechanism just running again per scope instead of running once — no additional pattern, just a different setting on the same machinery.

**Testing:** whether you can trace a container feature back to the plain pattern underneath it, instead of treating scope management as unexplained framework behavior.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: How the container manages object lifetime
